newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa closes Telkom sale to U.S.-Malaysian pair.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa closes Telkom sale to U.S.-Malaysian pair.

text.p: South African Telecommunications Minister Jay Naidoo on Wednesday formally closed the $1.26 billion sale of 30 percent of state utility Telkom to a U.S.-Malaysian consortium.

Naidoo signed the deal with Edward Whitacre, chairman of U.S.-based SBC Communications Inc, and Dato Mohamed Said Mohamad Ali, chief executive of Telekom Malaysia, who are acquiring the stake in the largest direct investment in South Africa to date.

Telkom Chairman Dikgang Moseneke said the consortium had pledged an extra 105 million rand ($23 million) for projects aimed at improving the quality of life for South Africa's impoverished black population.
"A truly remarkable and generous gesture that will contribute immensely in, among other things, expanding Internet usage and educating our people," Moseneke said.
"Our partners' commitment to support a five-year training budget of 2.3 billion rand...further underlines the depth of its intentinons to build long-term relationships with South Africa," he added.
Whitacre said the partnership generated great excitement within SBC.

"When we internally advertised for 50 assignments in South Africa we got more than 400 responses from people who wanted to come...You can rest assured you're getting our best and brightest," he said, adding that Mac Geschwind would serve as Telkom's chief operating officer.
"SBC's experience in Mexico is a textbook example of how a strong partnership can help transform a telecommunications monopoly into a responsive, customer-focused company.
"Aggressive expansion of a network to under-served areas can be accomplished, while at the same time providing acceptable returns to shareholders," Whitacre said.
"There is no question that South Africa is solidly positioned as the economic engine that will move southern Africa into the next century."
Naidoo said South Africa had a unique opportunity to become the hub of telecommunications in Africa.
"Our juxtaposition between East and West can catapult South Africa and Telkom onto the world stage, establishing the information backbone of the African Renaissance," he said.
Telkom plans to spend 53 billion rand over the next six years to install three million lines and replace 1.25 million analogue lines.
About $1.0 billion of the sale of the equity stake to the consortium will be spent on the infrastructure programme and the rest is expected to be used to retire state debt.
